# Fisher's Inequality

**Theorem.** Let $\mathcal D=(X,\mathcal B)$ be a balanced incomplete block design with parameters $(v,k,\lambda)$, i.e.

* $X$ is a set of $v$ points;
* $\mathcal B=(B_1,\dots,B_b)$ is a list of $b$ blocks, each $B_j\subseteq X$ with $\lvert B_j\rvert=k$ (repeated blocks are permitted);
* the design is *incomplete*: $k<v$;
* the design is *balanced*: there is an integer $\lambda\ge 1$ such that every $2$-subset $\{x,y\}\subseteq X$ is contained in exactly $\lambda$ blocks.

Then $b\ge v$.

Throughout, $I_v$ is the $v\times v$ identity matrix and $J_v$ the $v\times v$ all-ones matrix; all matrices are real.

Note first that $v\ge 2$: blocks are nonempty ($k\ge 1$, as is part of the definition of a block design), and $k<v$ then gives $v\ge 2$, so $X$ does contain $2$-subsets and the balance condition is not vacuous. (Many sources build $2\le k<v$ into the definition; we shall in fact *derive* $k\ge2$ in Step 1 from $k\ge1$, $v\ge2$ and $\lambda\ge1$.) Everything below uses only $v\ge2$, $1\le k<v$, $\lambda\ge1$.

## Step 1: the replication number is constant, and $k\ge 2$

Fix $x\in X$ and put
$$r_x:=\#\{j\in\{1,\dots,b\}: x\in B_j\}.$$
Count in two ways the set
$$P_x:=\{(y,j): y\in X\setminus\{x\},\ 1\le j\le b,\ \{x,y\}\subseteq B_j\}.$$

*Grouping by $y$.* For each of the $v-1$ points $y\ne x$, the pair $\{x,y\}$ lies in exactly $\lambda$ blocks, so $\lvert P_x\rvert=\lambda(v-1)$.

*Grouping by $j$.* If $x\in B_j$ then the admissible $y$ are the $k-1$ points of $B_j\setminus\{x\}$; if $x\notin B_j$ there are none. So $\lvert P_x\rvert=r_x(k-1)$.

Hence
$$r_x(k-1)=\lambda(v-1)\qquad\text{for every }x\in X. \tag{1}$$

Since $v\ge2$ and $\lambda\ge1$, the right-hand side of (1) is $\ge1>0$; therefore $k-1\ne0$, i.e. $k\ge 2$ (and $r_x\ge 1$). Consequently
$$r:=r_x=\frac{\lambda(v-1)}{k-1}$$
does not depend on $x$; $r$ is the *replication number*.

## Step 2: $r>\lambda$

From $2\le k<v$ we get $0<k-1<v-1$, so $\dfrac{v-1}{k-1}>1$ and
$$r=\lambda\cdot\frac{v-1}{k-1}>\lambda\ge 1. \tag{2}$$

(This is exactly where incompleteness, $k<v$, is used; for $k=v$ one has $r=\lambda$ and the theorem is false, e.g. $v=3$, $k=3$, $\lambda=1$, $b=1$.)

## Step 3: the incidence matrix and $NN^{\mathsf T}$

Write $X=\{x_1,\dots,x_v\}$ and let $N=(N_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{v\times b}$ be the incidence matrix,
$$N_{ij}=\begin{cases}1,& x_i\in B_j,\\ 0,&x_i\notin B_j.\end{cases}$$
For all $1\le i,h\le v$,
$$\bigl(NN^{\mathsf T}\bigr)_{ih}=\sum_{j=1}^{b}N_{ij}N_{hj}=\#\{j: x_i\in B_j\text{ and }x_h\in B_j\},$$
because $N_{ij}N_{hj}\in\{0,1\}$ equals $1$ exactly when $B_j$ contains both $x_i$ and $x_h$. For $i=h$ this count is $r_{x_i}=r$; for $i\ne h$ it is the number of blocks containing the pair $\{x_i,x_h\}$, namely $\lambda$. Therefore
$$NN^{\mathsf T}=(r-\lambda)I_v+\lambda J_v. \tag{3}$$

## Step 4: $NN^{\mathsf T}$ is nonsingular

Let $M:=(r-\lambda)I_v+\lambda J_v$ and let $z=(z_1,\dots,z_v)^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbb R^v$, $z\ne 0$. Since $z^{\mathsf T}J_vz=\bigl(\sum_i z_i\bigr)^2$,
$$z^{\mathsf T}Mz=(r-\lambda)\sum_{i=1}^{v}z_i^{2}+\lambda\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{v}z_i\Bigr)^{2}.$$
By (2) we have $r-\lambda>0$, and $\lambda\ge1>0$, so both summands are $\ge0$ and the first is $>0$ because $z\ne0$. Hence $z^{\mathsf T}Mz>0$ for all $z\ne0$: $M$ is positive definite, so $Mz\neq 0$ for $z\ne 0$ (if $Mz=0$ then $z^{\mathsf T}Mz=0$). Thus $M=NN^{\mathsf T}$ is invertible and
$$\operatorname{rank}\bigl(NN^{\mathsf T}\bigr)=v. \tag{4}$$

*Remark (determinant form).* Equivalently one may compute $\det M$. The all-ones matrix $J_v$ is symmetric with $J_v\mathbf 1=v\mathbf 1$ and $J_vz=0$ for every $z$ in the $(v-1)$-dimensional space $\{z:\sum_iz_i=0\}$; so $J_v$ has eigenvalues $v$ (once) and $0$ (with multiplicity $v-1$), and $M$ has eigenvalues $(r-\lambda)+\lambda v$ (once) and $r-\lambda$ (multiplicity $v-1$). Using (1) in the form $\lambda(v-1)=r(k-1)$,
$$\det M=\bigl(r+\lambda(v-1)\bigr)(r-\lambda)^{v-1}=\bigl(r+r(k-1)\bigr)(r-\lambda)^{v-1}=rk\,(r-\lambda)^{v-1}>0 .$$

## Step 5: conclusion

Every column of $NN^{\mathsf T}$ is an $\mathbb R$-linear combination of the columns of $N$ (the $j$-th column of $NN^{\mathsf T}$ is $N$ applied to the $j$-th column of $N^{\mathsf T}$), so the column space of $NN^{\mathsf T}$ is contained in that of $N$ and
$$\operatorname{rank}\bigl(NN^{\mathsf T}\bigr)\le\operatorname{rank}(N).$$
On the other hand $N$ has $b$ columns, so $\operatorname{rank}(N)\le b$. Combining with (4),
$$v=\operatorname{rank}\bigl(NN^{\mathsf T}\bigr)\le\operatorname{rank}(N)\le b .$$

Hence $b\ge v$. $\blacksquare$

**Corollary.** Since $bk=vr$ (count incidences two ways) and $b\ge v$, one also gets $r\ge k$.
